newsitem.title: USA: Clinton nominee Herman faces renewed criticism.
newsitem.headline: Clinton nominee Herman faces renewed criticism.

text.p: Labour Secretary-nominee Alexis Herman came under renewed attack Friday from a senior Republican congressman for her role in a controversial White House meeting among President Clinton, bankers and bank regulators.

Herman, then director of the White House Office of Public Liaison, added the name of Comptroller of the Currency Eugene Ludwig to the guest list for a May 13 coffee organised by the Democratic National Committee.
Herman said she only later realised the political nature of the coffee and decided not to attend herself. But Ludwig, charged with regulating U.S. banks, did attend.

"Alexis Herman realised the meeting was improper and did not attend," Representative Spencer Bachus, who chairs the House Banking Committee's Subcommittee on Oversight and Investigations, said. "Having recognised that fact, as a White House staffer, she should have told Mr. Ludwig that this was a meeting for political fund-raising purposes."
Herman's nomination is still pending before the Senate Labour Committee.

Senate Republican Leader Trent Lott said Friday he did not expect hearings on the nomination until after Congress returns from its President's Day recess in late February. Labour Committee members "are still working on some issues and getting some information they think is important," Lott said.

Clinton has conceded that Ludwig should not have attended the coffee. "In retrospect, since the DNC sponsored it I do not think the (Comptroller) of the Currency should have been there," Clinton said at a Jan. 28 press conference.
Since the controversy arose last month, Ludwig has repeatedly said he was not aware the meeting was a political event and would not have attended had he known.
Such coffees are only one of a series of questionable practices that have focused attention on the Clinton campaign's fundraising during last year's election.
The revelations have embarrassed Clinton, whose campaign returned more than $1.5 million in questionable contributions, while giving the Republicans a potent issue to attack him with.

Bachus, a Republican from Alabama, also said Friday he was disturbed that Ludwig's agency, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC), had helped the White House prepare for the meeting with bankers.

"I am particularly troubled by the extent to which the OCC was involved in preparing briefing materials and in planning the May 13 political fund-raising event at the White House," Bachus said after reviewing hundreds of pages of documents submitted by Ludwig Thursday.
"This is not a trivial matter," Bachus said. "Because it regulates all national banks, the actions of the OCC affect the financial security of every American family."
